q: How old must you be to apply for an Alberta Class 7 learner's licence?
why: You must be at least 14 years old.

q: What must a new Class 7 applicant under 18 have?
why: A parent or legal guardian must provide consent.

q: Which tests are required to obtain a Class 7 learner's licence?
why: A Class 7 applicant must pass a vision screening and the knowledge test.

q: How long must you hold a Class 7 licence before becoming eligible for Class 5-GDL?
why: The minimum learner stage is one year.

q: Who may supervise a Class 7 driver?
a: A fully licensed non-GDL driver age 18 or older seated beside the learner
why: The supervisor must be fully licensed, non-GDL, at least 18, and seated next to the learner.

q: When is a Class 7 learner prohibited from driving?
why: Class 7 learners may not drive between midnight and 5 a.m.

q: At how many demerit points is a Class 7 learner suspended?
why: Learners are suspended at eight or more demerit points.

q: What alcohol or drug level must a Class 7 driver have while driving?
why: Class 7 drivers must have zero alcohol and drug levels when driving.

q: How old must a learner be to qualify for Class 5-GDL?
why: The minimum age for Class 5-GDL is 16, after holding Class 7 for at least one year and passing the road test.

q: How many knowledge tests may a person take in one day?
why: The guide states that only one knowledge test may be taken per day.

q: At a solid red light, where must you stop?
a: Before the stop line or crosswalk
why: Stop before the stop line or crosswalk; if neither exists, stop before the intersection.

q: May you turn right at a red light in Alberta?
a: Yes, after a complete stop if no sign prohibits it and the way is safe
Only when another driver waves you through
why: Right on red is permitted after stopping, unless prohibited, while yielding to other traffic and pedestrians.

q: When may you turn left at a red light?
a: From any street onto a one-way street
Only from a one-way street onto a one-way street, after stopping and yielding
From a two-way street onto a one-way street
why: The only left turn permitted on red is from a one-way street onto a one-way street, unless prohibited.

q: A solid yellow light means:
a: Stop if it can be done safely; otherwise clear the intersection
why: Yellow warns that red is immediate. Stop unless you have reached a point where stopping cannot be done safely.

q: A flashing red light is treated like:
why: Stop completely, then proceed only when safe after yielding.

q: A flashing yellow light means:
a: Proceed with caution after yielding as necessary
why: Proceed cautiously and yield to pedestrians and vehicles within the intersection.

q: What does a red X above a lane mean?
a: Lane is closed to you or being used by oncoming traffic
why: Do not enter or remain in a lane displaying a red X.

q: What does a downward green arrow above a lane mean?
a: You may travel in that lane
why: A downward green arrow permits travel in that lane.

q: What does a red circle and slash over a symbol mean?
a: The action is permitted at night
why: A red circle and slash means the pictured action is prohibited.

q: What does a green circle on a white sign indicate?
why: A green circle indicates a permitted action.

q: What shape is commonly used for a warning sign?
why: Warning signs are generally yellow diamonds.

q: What colour is typically used for construction-area signs?
why: Construction information is generally shown on orange diamond-shaped signs.

q: Unless otherwise posted, what is the maximum speed on an urban roadway?
why: The general maximum is 50 km/h in an urban area, though municipalities may set different limits.

q: Unless otherwise posted, what is the maximum speed on a provincial highway outside an urban area?
why: The guide gives 100 km/h as the general maximum on a provincial highway outside an urban area.

q: A posted speed limit is:
a: The speed you must always drive
The maximum permitted only when conditions are ideal
why: A speed can still be illegal if it is unsafe for current conditions, even below the posted maximum.

q: A stop sign requires you to:
a: Slow and roll through if clear
Come to a complete stop and proceed only when safe
Stop only if traffic is present
why: A stop sign requires a full stop.

q: At a yield sign, you must yield to:
a: Traffic not facing the sign and pedestrians
why: Yield to traffic not facing the sign and to pedestrians waiting to cross or already within the crossing.

q: When flashing yellow lights at a pedestrian crossing are active, what maximum speed applies?
why: Reduce speed to a maximum of 30 km/h and yield or stop for pedestrians.

q: A school-zone sign is generally what shape?
why: School zone/area signs use a fluorescent yellow-green pentagon.

q: Before moving a vehicle, what should you do first?
a: Adjust seat, mirrors and restraints and check surroundings
why: Pre-drive preparation includes seating, mirrors, restraints, controls and a check around the vehicle.

q: When signalling a turn, the signal should be given:
a: Early enough to warn other road users
why: Signals communicate your intentions and must be given with enough time for others to respond.

q: When reversing, you should primarily look:
a: Through the rear window in the direction of travel while checking all around
why: Cameras and mirrors assist, but they do not replace looking in the direction the vehicle is moving and checking around it.

q: Why does stopping distance increase at higher speeds?
a: Both reaction distance and braking distance increase
why: The vehicle travels farther while the driver reacts and takes farther to brake as speed rises.

q: At an uncontrolled intersection, you should be prepared to yield to:
why: At an uncontrolled intersection, yield to the vehicle on your right when arrivals conflict.

q: Can you enter an intersection if traffic is backed up and you cannot clear it?
a: Yes, if the light is green
why: Do not enter unless you can clear the intersection.

q: When turning left, you normally must yield to:
a: Nobody when the light is green
why: A solid green permits movement, but left-turning drivers must yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

q: When entering a roundabout, you must yield to:
a: Only vehicles on your right outside it
why: Traffic already circulating has priority.

q: In a multi-lane turn, what should you do during and after the turn?
why: Maintain the lane indicated for your turn throughout the turn.

q: At a four-way stop, if two vehicles arrive at the same time, which normally goes first?
why: When arrival is simultaneous, the vehicle on the right normally proceeds first.

q: Before changing lanes, what sequence is safest?
a: Signal, mirror, shoulder check, move when safe
why: Signal your intention, check mirrors and blind spot, then move only when there is a safe gap.

q: When entering a freeway, you should generally:
a: Stop at the end of the acceleration lane
Use the acceleration lane to match traffic speed and merge into a safe gap
Enter at a very low speed
why: Use the acceleration lane to build an appropriate speed and merge safely; freeway traffic has priority.

q: On a two-lane highway, passing should be attempted only when:
a: It is legal and there is enough clear distance to complete it safely
The vehicle ahead is at the speed limit
You can exceed the speed limit
why: Passing is high-risk and must be both legal and safely completed within clear sight distance.

q: May you exceed the speed limit while passing?
why: The speed limit continues to apply while passing.

q: If your vehicle begins to skid, where should you look?
a: In the direction you want the vehicle to go
why: Look and steer toward your intended path while making smooth corrections.

q: In poor visibility or slippery conditions, you should:
a: Reduce speed and increase following distance
Follow closely so you can see the vehicle ahead
why: Conditions may require a speed well below the posted limit and more space to stop.

q: If a tire blows out, you should generally:
a: Hold the steering wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator and slow gradually
why: Maintain control and reduce speed gradually before moving off the road when safe.

q: When approaching an emergency vehicle stopped with lights flashing, you should:
a: Slow down and move over when safe as required
why: Protect roadside workers and responders by slowing and moving over safely.

q: What is proactive driving?
a: Continuously observing, anticipating hazards and taking action before problems develop
why: Proactive driving aims to prevent collisions through continuous observation and anticipation.

q: How many passengers may a Class 7 or Class 5-GDL driver carry?
a: No more than the number of seat belts
why: There may not be more passengers than available seat belts.

q: When a school bus has alternating red lights flashing, drivers must:
a: Stop as required and do not pass until the lights stop flashing
why: Flashing red school-bus lights require traffic to stop as prescribed; passing is dangerous and unlawful.

q: At a railway crossing, you should never:
why: Never enter unless you can completely clear the tracks.

q: Why should you give cyclists extra space?
a: They are vulnerable and may need room to avoid hazards
why: Cyclists are vulnerable road users and may need lateral space to deal with debris, doors and road conditions.

q: When following a large truck, why should you leave extra space?
a: To see around it and stay out of its blind spots
So another car can cut in
why: Large vehicles limit your view and have large blind spots; extra space improves visibility and safety.

q: What documents must a driver be able to produce when requested by a peace officer?
why: The driver must carry and produce a valid licence, insurance and registration.

q: Is it legal to operate an uninsured motor vehicle?
why: All motor vehicles must carry the required public-liability insurance.

q: What should a driver do about a medical condition that may affect safe driving?
a: Disclose it as required and provide medical documentation
why: The guide requires disclosure of medical or physical conditions that could affect safe operation.

q: The light is green, but cars are stopped across the intersection. What should Andy do?
a: Enter and wait in the intersection
Stay back until there is room to clear it
why: A green light does not permit blocking the intersection.

q: Andy reaches a yellow light and can stop smoothly before the line. What should he do?
why: A driver must stop for a solid yellow when stopping can be done safely.

q: Andy is driving below the posted limit during heavy rain. Is that automatically safe and legal?
a: No; he must choose a speed safe for conditions
why: Even a speed below the limit can be unsafe for current conditions.

q: A pedestrian is crossing the street Andy wants to turn into. What must he do?
a: Turn before the pedestrian reaches his lane
Yield and wait until the turn is safe
Drive behind them within the crosswalk
why: Turning drivers must yield to pedestrians in the crossing.

q: At an uncontrolled intersection, another vehicle approaches from Andy's right at the same time. What should Andy do?
a: Yield to the vehicle on the right
why: The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right when arrival conflicts.

q: Before moving a vehicle, what should you adjust first?
why: Adjust the seat, head restraint and mirrors so you can control the vehicle and see properly before moving.

q: When reversing, where should you primarily look?
a: In the direction the vehicle is moving, with frequent checks around the vehicle
why: Look mainly through the rear window in the direction of travel and continue checking all around. Cameras and mirrors are aids, not substitutes.

q: Why should you check behind the vehicle before getting in to reverse?
a: Small children or objects may be hidden from the driver's seat
It is required only on a road test
why: The area immediately behind a vehicle may not be visible from the driver's seat.

q: What following distance should normally be maintained in ideal conditions?
why: The guide recommends at least a two-second following distance in ideal conditions, increased when conditions are poor.

q: When conditions are poor, what should happen to your following distance?
a: It should stay exactly the same
why: Increase following distance when visibility, traction or stopping ability is reduced.

q: When following another vehicle within 150 metres at night, which headlights should you use?
why: Use low-beam headlights when following another vehicle within 150 metres.

q: When within 300 metres of an oncoming vehicle at night, which headlights should you use?
why: Use low beams when you are within 300 metres of an oncoming vehicle.

q: Why should high beams not be used in fog or heavy smoke?
a: The light reflects back and reduces visibility
They are illegal at all times
why: High beams reflect off fog, smoke or snow and can make it harder to see. Use low beams.

q: On an undivided roadway, what must traffic do when a school bus has alternating red lights flashing?
a: Only traffic behind the bus stops
why: On an undivided roadway, traffic approaching from both directions must stop for the school bus.

q: On a divided highway with a median, who must stop for a school bus with red lights flashing?
a: Only traffic behind the bus on the same side of the median
why: On a divided highway, vehicles behind the bus on its side of the median must stop; opposing traffic is separated by the median.

q: About how far from a stopped school bus should you stop?
why: The guide directs drivers to stop about 20 metres from the school bus.

q: When may you move again after stopping for a school bus?
a: As soon as the door closes
When the alternating red lights stop flashing
why: Remain stopped until the alternating flashing red lights are no longer operating.

q: When approaching a working snowplow, what is the safest general approach?
a: Follow closely so others cannot merge
Leave a large following distance and pass only when clearly safe and permitted
Use high beams in the snow cloud
why: Snowplows can create a snow cloud and spread sand or rocks. Leave plenty of space and do not pass unless it can be done safely.

q: What minimum following distance should you keep behind an emergency vehicle with its lights or siren operating?
why: The guide specifies a following distance of at least 150 metres behind an operating emergency vehicle.

q: Which is an example of distracted driving?
why: Using a hand-held cell phone while driving is prohibited distracted driving.

q: Who is responsible for ensuring the vehicle is insured and registered before it is driven?
a: The driver and vehicle owner must ensure legal requirements are met
why: A vehicle operated on Alberta roads must be properly registered and insured, and the required documents must be available.

q: Andy is behind a snowplow and cannot see through its snow cloud. What should he do?
a: Move closer to see its lights
Increase the gap and wait for visibility
why: Stay well back. The snow cloud can hide vehicles and road hazards, and the plow may spread sand or rocks.

q: At night, Andy is 100 metres behind another vehicle. What headlights should he use?
a: No lights if the road is lit
why: Within 150 metres of a vehicle ahead, use low-beam headlights.

q: Andy sees an emergency vehicle approaching with lights and siren. What should he do?
a: Yield, move safely out of its path and stop as required
why: Make room for the emergency vehicle, pull over safely and remain stopped until it has passed.

q: What is the minimum probationary period for a Class 5-GDL driver?
why: A Class 5-GDL driver must remain probationary for at least two years.

q: What is the minimum age to exit GDL and hold a full Class 5 licence?
why: A driver must be at least 18 and meet the other exit requirements.

q: To exit GDL, how long must the driver be free of suspensions or traffic violations at the end of probation?
why: The final 12 months of probation must be free of suspensions and traffic violations.

q: How much can approved driver training reduce the GDL probationary stage?
why: Approved driver education may reduce probation by up to six months when all conditions are met.

q: What endorsement shows completion of an approved driver education course?
why: Endorsement U records completion of an approved driver education course.

q: What should you bring to a vision assessment if you use corrective lenses?
why: Bring the corrective glasses or contacts you normally use.

q: About how long is the Alberta Class 5 road test, including instructions and the result summary?
why: The guide describes the Class 5 road test as approximately 45 minutes.

q: Which action is an automatic road-test failure?
a: Failing to stop completely at a stop sign
why: Failing to stop completely at a stop sign is listed as an automatic failure.

q: A Class 7 learner may operate a motorcycle only when the learner is at least:
why: A Class 7 holder must be at least 16 to learn on a motorcycle with a qualified Class 6 supervisor.

q: What is required to drive a vehicle equipped with air brakes?
why: An air-brake endorsement is required for vehicles with air-only or combined air/hydraulic braking systems.

q: What letter identifies the air-brake endorsement?
why: The Alberta air-brake endorsement is shown as Q.

q: Must a driver carry their licence while driving?
why: A driver must have the licence in their possession and produce it when requested.

q: What documents may a peace officer require from a driver?
why: Drivers must be able to produce their licence, insurance and registration.

q: Who must accompany a minor applying for a first Alberta driver’s licence?
why: A parent or legal guardian must attend, prove guardianship and sign consent unless an exemption applies.

q: Can a parent or guardian revoke consent for a minor’s licence before age 18?
why: The guardian may revoke consent in writing, causing the licence to be suspended.

q: How long may a new Alberta resident use an out-of-province licence after becoming resident?
why: A new Alberta resident must exchange the licence within 90 days.

q: What must a driver disclose if it could affect safe driving?
why: Conditions that may affect safe operation must be disclosed.

q: What condition code indicates adequate lenses are required?
why: Condition code A indicates adequate corrective lenses.

q: What does condition code H mean?
why: Condition H restricts the driver to daylight driving.

q: What does condition code K mean?
why: Condition K restricts the driver to an automatic transmission.

q: What must happen if a licence is lost, stolen, destroyed or unreadable?
why: The driver must apply for a replacement at a registry agent office.

q: Who is responsible for renewing a driver’s licence before it expires?
why: Renewal is the driver’s responsibility; general mailed reminders are no longer sent.

q: Are Alberta licence plates transferred to a new owner when a vehicle is sold?
a: No, plates remain with the owner
why: Alberta licence plates remain with the owner and are not transferable to another person.

q: What insurance is required for motor vehicles on Alberta roadways?
why: All motor vehicles must carry public liability insurance.

q: What is the order of lights on a vertical traffic signal from top to bottom?
why: Vertical signals place red at the top, yellow in the centre and green at the bottom.

q: What is the order of lights on a horizontal traffic signal from left to right?
why: Horizontal signals place red on the left, yellow in the centre and green on the right.

q: What does a green arrow shown with a red light permit?
a: Movement only in the arrow’s direction
why: The driver may proceed without stopping only in the direction of the green arrow.

q: What does a flashing green traffic light mean in Alberta?
a: You may proceed or turn, while still yielding to lawful road users
Treat it as a four-way stop
why: Opposing traffic faces red, but drivers must still yield to pedestrians or vehicles lawfully in the intersection.

q: When yellow pedestrian-crossing lights are flashing, what maximum speed applies?
why: Drivers must reduce speed to a maximum of 30 km/h and yield or stop for pedestrians.

q: A pedestrian who has already entered when DON’T WALK appears should:
why: A pedestrian already crossing may continue and clear the crosswalk.

q: What does an octagonal sign mean?
why: The eight-sided red sign means come to a complete stop.

q: What shape is a yield sign?
why: A yield sign is an inverted triangle.

q: What shape identifies a school zone or school area?
why: School-zone and school-area signs use a pentagon shape.

q: What does a yellow diamond sign generally indicate?
why: Yellow diamond signs warn of hazards or changing roadway conditions.

q: What do white symbols or words on a green rectangle usually provide?
why: Green guide signs provide directional and destination information.

q: What do white symbols or words on a blue sign usually indicate?
why: Blue information signs point to services such as fuel, food, lodging or assistance.

q: What does a WRONG WAY sign tell you?
a: Traffic is moving toward you in that direction
why: A WRONG WAY sign indicates that entering would place you against oncoming traffic.

q: At a yield sign, what must a driver do?
a: Ignore pedestrians outside a marked crosswalk
Yield to traffic and pedestrians with right-of-way
why: The driver must yield to traffic not facing the sign and to pedestrians waiting or crossing.

q: What does a DO NOT ENTER sign mean?
a: Do not enter the roadway or lane
why: The sign prohibits entry from that direction.

q: What does a black-and-white ONE WAY sign indicate?
a: Traffic travels only in the arrow’s direction
why: A one-way sign identifies the permitted direction of traffic flow.

q: What does a DIVIDED HIGHWAY BEGINS sign warn?
a: A median will separate opposing traffic
The roadway narrows to one lane
why: The sign warns that opposing traffic will soon be separated by a median.

q: What does a DIVIDED HIGHWAY ENDS sign warn?
a: Opposing traffic will no longer be separated by a median
why: The driver should prepare for opposing traffic on an undivided roadway.

q: What does a checkerboard sign usually mark?
a: The end of a roadway or a sharp change in direction
why: Checkerboard signs warn that the roadway ends or changes direction sharply.

q: What does a slow-moving vehicle emblem look like?
a: An orange triangle with a red border
why: Slow-moving vehicles display an orange triangle bordered in red.

q: When is a school-zone speed limit normally in effect unless local signs say otherwise?
a: On school days during posted times
Every day from sunrise to sunset
why: School-zone signs and local rules establish the applicable school-day times; drivers must follow the posted information.

q: What is the usual maximum speed in an Alberta playground zone unless otherwise posted?
why: The usual playground-zone maximum is 30 km/h during the times shown by law or sign.

q: May a driver pass another vehicle travelling in the same direction in a school or playground zone while the restriction is in effect?
a: Yes, if no children are visible
why: Passing another vehicle travelling in the same direction is prohibited while the zone restriction is in effect.

q: What do orange signs indicate?
why: Orange signs identify temporary construction and maintenance conditions.

q: What should a driver do when approaching a flag person in a construction zone?
a: Stop only if another driver stops
why: Flag persons have authority to direct traffic through a work zone.

q: Fines for speeding in a construction zone may be:
why: Construction zones may carry doubled speeding fines when workers are present, as indicated.

q: What does a solid yellow line separate?
a: Traffic moving in the same direction
A bicycle lane from a sidewalk
why: Yellow centre lines separate opposing traffic streams.

q: What does a solid white line generally separate?
a: Lanes moving in the same direction where lane changes are discouraged or restricted
A shoulder from a ditch only
why: White lines divide traffic moving in the same direction; a solid line signals that crossing is restricted or discouraged.

q: What does a broken white line mean?
a: Lane changes are permitted when safe
why: A broken white line separates same-direction lanes and may be crossed when safe.

q: What does a double solid yellow line mean?
a: Do not cross to pass in either direction
why: Double solid yellow lines prohibit crossing to pass in either direction.

q: What do white diamond pavement markings usually indicate?
why: Diamond symbols identify lanes reserved for specific users or vehicles.

q: What does a painted bicycle symbol in a lane indicate?
a: A bicycle lane or shared-use facility
why: The bicycle symbol identifies a lane or roadway space intended for bicycle use.

q: What is a shared-use lane marking sometimes called?
why: A bicycle symbol with chevrons is commonly called a sharrow and reminds users to share the lane.

q: Before driving, what should be adjusted first for a safe seating position?
why: A safe pre-drive setup includes correct seating, head restraint and mirror adjustment.

q: Where should the top of the head restraint be positioned?
a: At the base of the neck
At least level with the top of the ears
why: The restraint should support the head and be at least as high as the top of the ears.

q: Why should loose objects be secured before driving?
a: They can become dangerous projectiles in a sudden stop or collision
why: Unsecured cargo can strike occupants during sudden movement.

q: What should you check around the vehicle before getting in?
a: Nothing if the vehicle has a camera
Children, animals, obstacles, leaks and vehicle condition
why: A walk-around can reveal hazards, obstacles or mechanical problems cameras may miss.

q: What is the purpose of the parking brake?
a: To help secure a parked vehicle
To stop faster at highway speed
why: The parking brake helps keep a parked vehicle from moving.

q: When moving an automatic transmission from Park, what should you normally do?
why: The brake should be applied while selecting a drive gear.

q: What does engine braking mean?
a: Using a lower gear to help reduce speed
Turning the engine off while moving
why: A lower gear lets engine resistance assist with slowing, especially on long grades.

q: For ordinary steering, where should the hands generally be placed?
a: One hand on the gear selector
why: A balanced 9-and-3 position supports control and reduces airbag-related injury risk.

q: When should a turn signal be used?
a: Before turning, changing lanes, pulling away or moving to the curb
Only when another vehicle is close
why: Signals communicate intended movement to other road users.

q: Does signalling give a driver the right-of-way?
a: Only if signalling for three seconds
why: A signal communicates intent; the driver must still ensure the movement is safe and yield as required.

q: What is the safest way to accelerate from a stop?
a: By looking only in the rear-view mirror
why: Smooth acceleration preserves traction and gives others time to respond.

q: What three factors make up total stopping distance?
why: Total stopping distance includes seeing the hazard, reacting and the vehicle’s braking distance.

q: What happens to stopping distance as speed increases?
why: Higher speed increases both distance travelled during reaction and braking distance.

q: Which condition increases stopping distance?
why: Reduced traction increases the distance needed to stop.

q: When reversing, where should you look?
a: In the direction of travel, using mirrors and direct observation
why: Drivers must look behind and around the vehicle; cameras are aids, not substitutes for observation.

q: When backing from a driveway, who must you yield to?
a: Pedestrians and traffic on the roadway
why: A vehicle entering a roadway from private property must yield to road users and pedestrians.

q: What is the safest choice when visibility behind the vehicle is poor?
a: Get out and check or use a guide when appropriate
why: Confirming the path is clear prevents backing collisions.

q: When parallel parking, how close should the vehicle generally be to the curb?
why: The guide requires the vehicle to be parked close to and parallel with the curb, generally within 50 cm.

q: When parking uphill with a curb, which way should the front wheels point?
why: If the vehicle rolls backward, the tire should catch the curb.

q: When parking downhill with a curb, which way should the front wheels point?
why: Turning toward the curb helps prevent the vehicle from rolling into traffic.

q: When parking uphill without a curb, which way should the wheels point?
a: Toward the edge of the road
why: Turn toward the road edge so a rolling vehicle moves away from traffic.

q: Before leaving a parked vehicle, what should you do?
a: Set the parking brake and secure the transmission
why: The vehicle should be secured against movement before occupants leave.

q: Is parking permitted in front of a driveway?
why: Parking must not block a driveway.

q: Is parking permitted on a crosswalk?
a: Yes if no pedestrians are present
why: A vehicle must not be parked on a crosswalk.

q: What is angle parking?
a: Parking at an angle to the curb in marked spaces
why: Angle parking uses spaces marked diagonally or at right angles to the curb.

q: Who has right-of-way when entering a roadway from an alley, driveway or parking lot?
a: Traffic and pedestrians already on the roadway or sidewalk
why: A driver entering from private property must yield to road users and pedestrians.

q: At an uncontrolled intersection, who normally yields when two vehicles arrive at about the same time?
a: The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right
The driver on the right yields to the left
why: At an uncontrolled intersection, yield to the vehicle on your right when arrivals are approximately simultaneous.

q: At a four-way stop, who normally proceeds first?
why: The first vehicle to stop is normally first to proceed, after confirming it is safe.

q: At a four-way stop when two vehicles stop at the same time, who yields?
a: The vehicle turning right always yields
The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right
The driver on the right yields to the left
why: The same-time rule requires the driver on the left to yield to the driver on the right.

q: May you enter an intersection if traffic is backed up and you cannot clear it?
a: Yes if the light is green
Yes if you are turning right
why: Do not block an intersection; wait until there is room beyond it.

q: What is the key rule when entering a roundabout?
a: Yield to traffic already in the roundabout
Traffic in the roundabout yields to entering traffic
why: Entering drivers yield to vehicles already circulating and to pedestrians as required.

q: Which direction does traffic move in an Alberta roundabout?
a: It changes by time of day
why: Traffic circulates counter-clockwise around the centre island.

q: Should you change lanes inside a roundabout?
a: Avoid it; choose the correct lane before entering
why: Drivers should select the proper lane before entering and maintain it through the roundabout.

q: When should you signal in a roundabout?
why: A right signal communicates the intended exit.

q: When turning right, which lane should you normally enter?
a: The first available lane to the right
why: Complete the turn into the nearest lawful lane unless signs or markings direct otherwise.

q: When turning left from a two-way road onto a two-way road, which lane should you enter?
a: The lane immediately to the right of the centre line
why: A left turn should normally end in the nearest lawful lane on the new roadway.

q: Before turning left, what must you yield to?
a: No one when the light is green
why: A green light does not remove the duty to yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians while turning left.

q: What is a two-way left-turn lane used for?
a: Left turns by vehicles travelling in either direction
why: The centre lane is shared for preparing and completing left turns, not for general travel or passing.

q: May you travel for a long distance in a two-way left-turn lane?
why: The lane is for turning movements, not through travel.

q: When may a U-turn be made?
a: On a curve with limited visibility
why: U-turns are restricted and must only be made where permitted and safe.

q: Is a U-turn permitted at a traffic-light-controlled intersection unless a sign allows it?
why: U-turns at signal-controlled intersections are prohibited unless a sign specifically permits them.

q: Is a U-turn permitted on a curve or near the crest of a hill when visibility is limited?
why: Limited sight distance makes a U-turn unsafe and prohibited.

q: On a multi-lane highway, which lane should slower traffic generally use?
why: Keep right except when passing, turning left or when lane use requires otherwise.

q: What should you do before changing lanes?
a: Check mirrors, signal and shoulder-check the blind spot
why: A safe lane change requires observation, signalling and a blind-spot check.

q: When passing another vehicle, when should you return to your lane?
a: Only after slowing below its speed
When you can see the passed vehicle in your inside rear-view mirror and it is safe
As soon as your front bumper is ahead
why: Leave enough clearance before moving back into the lane.

q: Where is passing prohibited?
a: Where signs or pavement markings prohibit it or sight distance is insufficient
why: Do not pass when prohibited or where you cannot see far enough to complete the manoeuvre safely.

q: What should a driver being passed do?
a: Maintain a steady speed and allow the pass
why: A steady, predictable speed helps the passing vehicle complete the manoeuvre safely.

q: What is the emergency stopping lane or highway shoulder intended for?
a: Emergencies and stopped vehicles, not ordinary travel
why: The shoulder is not a normal travel or passing lane.

q: When entering a freeway, where should you build speed?
a: At the end of the ramp while stopped
why: Use the acceleration lane to match the speed of freeway traffic before merging.

q: Who has right-of-way when you merge onto a freeway?
why: The entering driver must find a safe gap and yield to traffic already on the major roadway.

q: What should you do if you miss a freeway exit?
a: Make a U-turn through the median
why: Never stop or reverse; continue safely to the next exit.

q: When leaving a freeway, when should you reduce speed?
a: After entering the deceleration lane, unless conditions require earlier action
In the through lane before the exit
why: Move into the exit lane first, then slow according to the ramp and conditions.

q: Why should you leave extra space behind a large truck?
a: To prevent the truck from changing lanes
To improve visibility and stay out of its blind spot
why: Extra distance improves sight lines and gives more time to respond.

q: If emergency braking is needed in a vehicle with ABS, what should you do?
a: Press the brake firmly and keep steady pressure
Release the brake whenever it vibrates
why: ABS may pulse; maintain firm pressure and steer where you want to go.

q: If a vehicle without ABS begins to skid during hard braking, what should you do?
a: Ease brake pressure enough to regain steering, then brake again
Press harder and lock the wheels
why: Locked wheels cannot steer; controlled braking helps regain traction.

q: If the rear wheels skid, where should you steer?
a: In the direction you want the front of the vehicle to go
Directly opposite the skid at all times
why: Look and steer toward the intended path while easing off the cause of the skid.

q: What is the first response to hydroplaning?
a: Ease off the accelerator and steer smoothly
why: Sudden braking or steering can worsen loss of traction; reduce speed smoothly.

q: If a front tire blows out, what should you do?
a: Hold the steering wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator and slow gradually
why: Maintain control and reduce speed gradually before moving off the roadway.

q: If the accelerator sticks, what should you do?
a: Shift to neutral, brake and move safely off the road
Turn the key to steering lock immediately
Pump the accelerator and speed up
why: Neutral disconnects engine power from the wheels; then brake and stop safely.

q: If the brakes fail, which action may help slow the vehicle?
a: Shift to a lower gear and carefully use the parking brake
why: Downshifting and controlled parking-brake use may reduce speed while seeking a safe escape path.

q: If the engine overheats, what should you avoid doing immediately?
why: Opening a hot cooling system can release scalding steam or coolant.

q: In fog, which headlights should you use?
why: High beams reflect off fog and reduce visibility; low beams are more effective.

q: At night, how should speed relate to headlight visibility?
a: Drive slowly enough to stop within the illuminated distance
Drive at the posted limit regardless of visibility
Use high beams in all traffic
why: You must be able to stop within the distance you can see.

q: What should you do when approaching glare from oncoming headlights?
a: Look toward the right edge of your lane and reduce speed
why: Using the right road edge as a guide helps avoid glare while maintaining lane position.

q: What should you do on icy or snowy roads?
a: Follow closely to use tire tracks
Reduce speed, increase following distance and make smooth inputs
why: Low traction requires more space and gentle steering, acceleration and braking.

q: Should cruise control be used on slippery roads?
why: Cruise control can worsen wheel spin or loss of control on slippery surfaces.

q: What is black ice?
a: A thin, often nearly invisible layer of ice
why: Black ice can be difficult to see and dramatically reduces traction.

q: Where may icy conditions form first?
why: Elevated and shaded surfaces often cool and freeze before surrounding pavement.

q: If an animal appears on the road, what should you generally do?
a: Brake firmly while maintaining control and avoid a dangerous swerve
why: A sudden swerve may cause a more serious collision; controlled braking is usually safer.

q: What emergency supplies are useful in winter?
a: Warm clothing, blanket, flashlight, food, water and traction aids
No supplies are needed in cities
why: A winter emergency kit helps occupants remain safe if stranded.

q: After a collision, what is the first priority?
a: Protect people and prevent further collisions
why: Secure the scene, assess injuries and call for help as required.

q: Should a seriously injured person be moved after a collision?
a: Only when necessary to protect them from immediate danger
why: Unnecessary movement can worsen injuries; move only to escape an immediate hazard.

q: What should drivers do when an emergency vehicle approaches with lights or siren?
a: Yield and move safely to the side, then stop
why: Drivers must clear a path and stop safely for the emergency vehicle.

q: After an emergency vehicle passes, how closely may you follow?
a: Do not follow closely; keep the legally required distance
why: Following closely is dangerous and prohibited; maintain a substantial safe distance.

q: When passing a stopped emergency or tow vehicle with flashing lights, what should you do?
a: Move over when safe and slow to the required speed
Maintain speed in the nearest lane
why: Alberta’s roadside-worker rules require drivers to slow and, where possible, move away from the stopped vehicle.

q: What should you do around snowplows and road-maintenance vehicles?
a: Give them extra room and do not pass unless it is clearly safe
Follow closely for a clearer road
why: These vehicles may create snow clouds, spread material and have large blind spots.

q: How far ahead should a driver scan in an urban area?
why: Looking well ahead gives time to identify changing traffic and hazards.

q: What is a space cushion?
a: Open space maintained around the vehicle
why: Space around the vehicle provides escape options and reaction time.

q: What minimum following interval is commonly recommended in good conditions?
why: A minimum three-second interval gives basic reaction space in favourable conditions.

q: When should following distance be increased?
a: Only when driving below the limit
In poor weather, darkness, heavy traffic or when following large vehicles
why: Reduced visibility, traction or sight lines require extra time and space.

q: What should you do if another driver is following too closely?
a: Increase space ahead and allow them to pass when safe
why: More space ahead lets you slow gradually and reduces the chance of being rear-ended.

q: Why should drivers check mirrors regularly?
a: Because mirrors remove all blind spots
To maintain awareness of traffic beside and behind them
why: Mirror checks are part of continuous 360-degree awareness, but shoulder checks are still needed.

q: What is a blind spot?
a: An area around the vehicle not visible in mirrors
why: Mirrors do not show every area beside and behind a vehicle.

q: Who must wear a seat belt when one is available?
why: Drivers must ensure passengers are properly secured, and all occupants must use available restraints.

q: Who is responsible for ensuring passengers under 16 are properly restrained?
why: The driver is responsible for passengers under age 16.

q: Where is the safest place for most children under 13?
why: The rear seat generally provides better protection from frontal impact and airbags.

q: What child restraint should be used?
a: A booster only for every child
One appropriate for the child’s age, weight and height and installed correctly
Any adult seat belt from birth
why: Child restraints must match the child and be used according to manufacturer and legal requirements.

q: May passengers ride in a trailer being towed?
why: A towed trailer is not a safe passenger compartment.

q: Which driving habit improves fuel efficiency and safety?
why: Smooth, planned driving reduces fuel use and abrupt manoeuvres.

q: What should you do before opening a vehicle door into traffic?
a: Check mirrors and the blind spot for cyclists and vehicles
why: A door can seriously injure a cyclist or obstruct traffic.

q: Who is considered a vulnerable road user?
why: Vulnerable users have less physical protection in a collision.

q: At a marked or unmarked crosswalk, what must drivers do for pedestrians?
a: Proceed if there is no traffic light
why: Drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing or indicating an intention to cross where required.

q: May you pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian?
why: The stopped vehicle may be shielding a pedestrian from view.

q: How much room should you give a cyclist when passing?
a: As much space as practical and legally required
No extra room in a marked lane
why: Cyclists may need to avoid debris or wind; pass only with ample safe clearance.

q: Why should you check for cyclists before turning right?
a: A cyclist may be travelling straight beside you
Cyclists must always stop behind cars
why: A cyclist on the right may be hidden in a blind spot and may have right-of-way.

q: What should a driver do before crossing a bicycle lane to turn?
a: Stop in the bicycle lane and wait
Use the lane as a passing lane
Check, signal and yield to cyclists
why: Drivers must cross bicycle facilities only when safe and yield to users already there.

q: Why are motorcycles easy to misjudge?
a: Their smaller size can make speed and distance difficult to estimate
why: Small visual size can make an approaching motorcycle seem farther away or slower than it is.

q: Should a motorcycle be given a full lane?
a: No, cars may share beside it
why: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane and may need room to avoid hazards.

q: Where are a large truck’s blind spots?
a: In front, behind and along both sides, especially the right side
why: Large vehicles have extensive no-zones around the cab and trailer.

q: Why should you not cut closely in front of a large truck?
a: It can stop faster than a car
The driver sits too low to see you
It needs much more distance to stop
why: Heavy vehicles require long stopping distances and may lose sight of a vehicle close ahead.

q: When a truck turns right, why might it first move left?
a: To create room for the trailer to clear the corner
To let cars pass on the right
why: Long vehicles often swing wide; never squeeze between the truck and curb.

q: What should you do when meeting a school bus with alternating red lights flashing on an undivided road?
a: Stop only if children are visible
Only traffic behind the bus stops
why: On an undivided road, traffic approaching from either direction must stop for the flashing red lights.

q: On a divided highway, who must stop for a school bus with flashing red lights?
a: Traffic travelling behind the bus on its side of the divided highway
why: The physical divider separates opposing traffic; vehicles behind the bus on its roadway must stop.

q: What do alternating amber lights on a school bus warn?
a: The bus is safe to pass
The bus is out of service
The bus is preparing to stop
why: Amber lights warn drivers that the bus is slowing and will soon activate red stopping lights.

q: When approaching a railway crossing, what should you do?
a: Look and listen in both directions and be prepared to stop
Stop on the tracks if traffic backs up
why: A train may approach at any time, even where warning devices are absent or malfunctioning.

q: May you drive around lowered railway gates?
a: Yes if no train is visible
why: Never drive around or under a lowered gate.

q: When must you avoid entering a railway crossing?
a: Only when a train horn sounds
When there is not enough room to clear the tracks completely
why: Never stop on the tracks; wait until there is enough space beyond them.

q: Why should you expect more than one train at a multiple-track crossing?
a: Signals apply to only one train
A second train may be hidden by the first
why: After one train passes, another may approach on a different track.

q: What should you do when approaching a snowplow producing a snow cloud?
a: Slow down and stay well back
Follow closely in the cleared path
why: The cloud can hide the plow and other traffic; visibility and traction may be poor.

q: What should drivers do near a funeral procession?
a: Show courtesy and avoid cutting through it
Join it to bypass traffic lights
why: Funeral processions should be treated respectfully and not disrupted.

q: What should you expect from a person using a white cane or guide dog?
a: They must yield to all vehicles
They can see traffic lights normally
They may have limited or no vision and must be given time and right-of-way
why: Drivers must recognize mobility aids and yield patiently to pedestrians with visual impairments.

q: What is the safest approach around horseback riders or livestock on a road?
a: Drive close so the animal sees you
Slow down, give wide clearance and avoid sudden noise
why: Animals may startle; quiet, slow and predictable movement reduces risk.

q: What should a driver do if tired or drowsy?
a: Stop in a safe place and rest
Open a window and continue indefinitely
Turn up music and speed up
Use a phone to stay alert
why: Fatigue impairs driving; rest is the effective response.

q: Can prescription or over-the-counter medication affect driving?
why: Many medicines can cause drowsiness, slowed reactions or impaired judgment.

q: What should you do before driving after taking medication?
a: Read warnings and ask a pharmacist or health professional if uncertain
Assume it is safe because it is legal
why: Legal medication can still impair driving ability.

q: Is using a hand-held phone while driving permitted?
why: Alberta distracted-driving law prohibits hand-held electronic-device use while driving, including while stopped in traffic.

q: Does being stopped at a red light allow hand-held phone use?
why: A driver stopped in traffic is still driving for distracted-driving purposes.

q: Which activity can be distracted driving even without a phone?
a: Any activity that takes attention from driving
why: Distraction includes visual, manual and cognitive activities that reduce driving attention.

q: What is the safest rule regarding alcohol, cannabis or impairing drugs before driving?
why: Impairing substances reduce judgment, reaction and coordination; the safe choice is not to drive.

q: Can cannabis impair driving even if it is legal?
why: Legality does not remove impairment risk or driving prohibitions.

q: What should you do if you are angry or emotionally upset?
a: Calm down before driving or stop safely
why: Strong emotion can impair attention, judgment and risk perception.

q: What is aggressive driving?
a: Driving below the limit in snow
Unsafe behaviour motivated by impatience, hostility or competition
why: Aggressive driving includes tailgating, unsafe lane changes, speeding and hostile actions.

q: How should you respond to an aggressive driver?
a: Avoid engagement, create distance and let them go
why: Do not escalate; protect space and report serious danger when safe.

q: What is the purpose of demerit points?
a: To identify and sanction repeated traffic violations
why: Demerits accumulate for convictions and can lead to suspension.

q: What can happen if a learner or probationary driver reaches 8 demerit points?
why: Class 7 and Class 5-GDL drivers are suspended at eight or more demerit points.

q: Must you obey directions from a peace officer even if traffic signals indicate something else?
why: A peace officer directing traffic overrides ordinary signs and signals.

q: What should you do after receiving a licence suspension notice?
a: Ask a passenger to watch for police
Stop driving as directed and comply with reinstatement requirements
Continue until the licence card expires
why: Driving while suspended is unlawful and can lead to further penalties.

q: What is SafeRoads Alberta associated with?
a: Administrative sanctions for impaired driving and related matters
why: SafeRoads Alberta administers provincial impaired-driving sanctions and review processes.

q: Must a trailer travelling on Alberta roadways be registered?
why: Motor vehicles and trailers operated on roadways must be registered.

q: Where must the trailer licence plate be displayed?
a: Securely at the rear and clearly visible
why: The plate must be attached at the rear and visible as required.

q: What must connect a trailer to the tow vehicle in addition to the main hitch?
why: Safety chains or cables provide a backup connection if the hitch fails.

q: How should safety chains be attached?
a: Crossed under the trailer tongue with enough slack for turns
why: Crossing the chains can cradle the tongue and they must permit normal turning without dragging.

q: What should be checked before towing?
a: Hitch, coupler, chains, lights, tires, load and brakes if equipped
why: A complete pre-trip check helps prevent separation, tire failure and lighting or load problems.

q: How should cargo in a trailer be loaded?
a: Evenly distributed and securely tied down
why: Balanced, secured cargo improves stability and prevents shifting.

q: What may happen if too much trailer weight is placed at the rear?
a: The tow vehicle will stop faster
why: Insufficient tongue weight can make the trailer unstable and prone to sway.

q: What should you do if a trailer begins to sway?
a: Apply the tow vehicle parking brake
Ease off the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt braking
why: Smoothly reducing speed helps restore stability; abrupt inputs can worsen sway.

q: Why is extra following distance needed when towing?
a: The combination is heavier and takes longer to stop
The trailer makes the vehicle narrower
The speed limit no longer applies
why: Added mass increases stopping distance and reduces manoeuvrability.

q: What should you remember when turning with a trailer?
a: Make the turn as sharply as possible
The trailer tracks inside the tow vehicle’s path, so turns need extra room
The trailer turns outside every curve
why: Off-tracking means trailer wheels cut closer to the inside of the turn.

q: Before backing a trailer, what is helpful?
a: Plan the path, use mirrors and a spotter when available
why: Backing is easier and safer with a planned path, slow movement and clear communication.

q: May passengers ride in a travel trailer while it is being towed?
why: Passengers must ride in an approved seating position in the tow vehicle, not in the trailer.

q: On a multi-lane highway, where should slower traffic normally travel?
a: In whichever lane has the fewest vehicles
why: Slower traffic should normally use the travel lane furthest to the right, leaving the left lane available for passing.

q: Your mirrors show no vehicle beside you. Is that enough information to change lanes?
a: Yes, mirrors show every nearby vehicle
No, you must also shoulder check for vehicles or cyclists in the blind spot
why: Mirrors do not show all areas beside and slightly behind the vehicle. A shoulder check is required before changing lanes.

q: When changing lanes, what should you do with your speed if conditions allow?
a: Maintain your speed as much as possible
Coast until the lane change is complete
why: A safe lane change is made smoothly while maintaining speed as much as possible.

q: Which check looks into the area your mirrors cannot show before a lane change?
why: A quick shoulder check through the rear side window reveals the blind spot.

q: After completing a lane change, what should you confirm?
a: The signal light has turned off
The headlights are on high beam
why: After moving into the lane, make sure the turn signal is cancelled.

q: Why should the left lane generally be kept available on a multi-lane highway?
why: Keeping slower traffic to the right leaves the left lane available for passing.

q: A highway passing lane is ending. What must drivers in the right lane do?
a: Stop at the end of the lane
Merge safely with traffic to the left
why: Drivers in the ending right lane must merge safely; drivers in the left lane should cooperate.

q: You are in the left lane when a passing lane ends and vehicles on the right need to merge. What should you do?
a: Cooperate and allow a safe merge
why: Drivers in the left lane should cooperate so traffic from the ending right lane can merge safely.

q: When should you pass on a two-lane highway?
a: Whenever the vehicle ahead is below the speed limit
Only where legal, necessary and safe, with no oncoming traffic for a safe distance
Whenever the centre line is visible
Only when another driver follows you closely
why: Two-lane passing is dangerous and should be attempted only where permitted and when it can be completed safely.

q: May you exceed the speed limit briefly to complete a pass?
a: Yes, if the road is clear
No, exceeding the speed limit while passing is illegal
why: The speed limit still applies while passing another vehicle.

q: Another vehicle is passing you on a two-lane highway. What is the safest response?
a: Stay in your lane and move toward the right side of it
why: Stay in your lane and move toward the right side to improve the passing driver's view ahead.

q: What does a solid yellow line on your side of the centre line mean for passing?
why: Do not pass when a solid yellow line is on your side of the centre line.

q: A vehicle ahead has stopped for a pedestrian at an unmarked crosswalk. May you pass it?
a: Yes, if you cannot see the pedestrian
why: It is illegal and dangerous to pass a vehicle stopped to allow a pedestrian to cross.

q: When must you not pass a stopped school bus?
a: When its red lights are flashing and stop arm is extended
Only when it is facing your direction
why: Flashing red lights and an extended stop arm indicate that traffic must stop as required.

q: What is the emergency stopping lane on a primary highway intended for?
why: The shoulder or emergency stopping lane is for urgent situations and vehicle problems.

q: May you use the emergency stopping lane to help another vehicle pass you?
why: Do not drive in the emergency stopping lane or use it to pass or assist another driver to pass.

q: Who has the right-of-way when a merging lane joins a highway?
a: Neither automatically; merging is a shared responsibility
why: The guide describes merging as a shared responsibility between vehicles joining and vehicles already on the roadway.

q: What should you generally avoid doing in an acceleration lane?
why: Acceleration lanes are designed to let you reach highway speed. Abrupt slowing or stopping may lead to a rear-end collision.

q: As soon as you can see the highway lane you will enter, what should you begin doing?
a: Choosing a gap and adjusting your speed
Stopping at the end of the ramp
why: Identify a suitable gap early and adjust speed and timing to blend smoothly with traffic.

q: When should you move from the acceleration lane into the highway gap?
a: Before the solid white line ends
After you are past the solid white line, when safe and legal
Only after slowing below traffic speed
why: Merge after passing the solid white line, when the gap is safe and legal, while maintaining traffic speed.

q: You are on the main highway and traffic is entering from a merge lane. What can you do if it is safe?
a: Move left to leave the right lane clear
Speed up to close all gaps
why: Moving left when safe can provide room for merging traffic.

q: When should you move into the proper lane for a highway exit?
why: Plan ahead and be in the correct lane well before the exit.

q: Where should you normally begin reducing speed for a highway exit?
a: After moving into the deceleration lane
On the shoulder before the exit
Only at the end of the ramp
why: Move into the deceleration lane first, then slow to the posted safe ramp speed.

q: You realize too late that your exit is beside you. What should you do?
why: Do not make a sudden turn or stop. Continue safely and use the next exit.

q: Why do weave zones require extra caution?
a: Entering and exiting vehicles share the same lane while changing speed and position
Only commercial vehicles may use them
why: In a weave zone, some drivers are slowing to exit while others are accelerating to enter, requiring cooperation and space.

q: In an emergency stop with ABS, how should you apply the brake pedal?
a: Press firmly and hold while steering as needed
why: With ABS, use firm continuous brake pressure and steer toward a safe path; do not pump the brakes.

q: When recovering from a skid, where should you look and steer?
a: In the direction you want the front of the vehicle to go
why: Look and steer toward the intended path of the front of the vehicle.

q: A vehicle without ABS enters a braking skid because its wheels lock. What should the driver do first?
a: Take the foot off the brake so the wheels can roll and steering can return
why: Releasing the brake lets the wheels roll again and restores steering control.

q: Your vehicle begins sliding sideways in a corner because you entered too fast. What should you do?
a: Take your foot off the gas, avoid braking, and steer where you want to go
why: For a cornering skid, ease off the gas, do not brake, and look and steer toward the intended path.

q: Your right wheels leave the pavement. What should you do first?
a: Steer sharply back onto the road
Keep a firm grip and reduce speed without immediately steering back
Accelerate to climb back onto the pavement
why: Do not jerk the vehicle back. Hold the wheel firmly, ease off the gas and return gradually when speed and traffic conditions permit.

q: Before gradually steering back onto the road after leaving the pavement, what must you check?
why: Check for traffic before returning gradually to the proper travel lane.

q: Where should you avoid stopping for a mechanical problem if at all possible?
why: Stopping on a bridge or in a tunnel is especially dangerous.

q: Your disabled vehicle is left in a potentially dangerous location. Which actions help make it visible?
a: Turn off all lights and close the hood
Turn on hazard lights and raise the hood
why: Use hazard lights and raise the hood; reflective triangles may also be placed safely behind the vehicle.

q: On a highway, approximately how far apart should reflective triangles be placed behind a disabled vehicle?
why: The guide recommends placing reflective triangles about 10 to 20 metres apart to the rear when it can be done safely.

q: A vehicle is stopped in a potentially dangerous highway location. Where should occupants wait if they must leave it?
a: Directly in front of the vehicle
At a safe location to the rear and away from the vehicle
why: Move away from traffic and wait to the rear and away from the vehicle, not in the danger area beside it.

q: The brake warning light stays on after you confirm the park brake is released. What should you do?
a: Continue until the next fuel stop
Move to the side of the road as soon as it is safe
why: A brake warning light may indicate a serious problem; move safely off the road.

q: Your engine stops and power-brake assistance is lost. The vehicle does not slow with normal pedal pressure. What should you do?
a: Push the brake pedal harder with steady pressure
Turn off the ignition and remove the key
why: Without power assistance, the brakes may still work but require harder, steady pedal pressure.

q: If the service brakes fail and the wheels are not turned, what may help slow the vehicle?
a: Carefully using the park brake and shifting to a lower gear
Turning sharply from side to side
why: A carefully applied park brake and a lower gear may help bring the vehicle to a controlled stop.

q: Can a vehicle still be steered if power steering fails?
a: Yes, but much more effort is required
why: Mechanical steering remains, but turning the wheel will require extra effort.

q: A tire suddenly goes flat while you are driving. What should you resist doing immediately?
a: Looking where you want to go
why: Immediate braking can worsen loss of control. Ease off the gas, hold a straight course and brake gently after speed is reduced.

q: What may happen when a front tire goes flat?
a: The vehicle pulls strongly toward the flat tire
The vehicle always turns away from it
why: A flat front tire can cause a strong pull toward the side of the failed tire.

q: After controlling a vehicle with a flat tire and moving safely off the road, what should you turn on?
why: Hazard lights help warn approaching drivers that the vehicle is stopped.

q: Both headlights fail at night. What should you try first after turning on the hazard lights?
a: Turn the headlight control off and on
Speed up to reach a lit area
Drive in the centre of the road
why: Turn on the hazards, cycle the headlight control, and if the lights remain off, slow and park safely.

q: When must headlights be on because of limited visibility?
a: Whenever you cannot clearly see 150 metres ahead
Only when street lights are off
why: Headlights are required at night and whenever you cannot clearly see 150 metres in front.

q: Why are daytime running lights not enough for night driving?
a: They may not turn on the tail-lights and instrument-panel lights and are not bright enough
why: Daytime running lights do not provide full night lighting and may leave rear and instrument lights off.

q: Should you use low-beam headlights when there is oncoming traffic on a divided highway?
a: No, the median blocks all glare
Only if the other driver flashes their lights
why: Use low beams for oncoming traffic even when the highway is divided.

q: How should you reduce glare from approaching headlights?
a: Look slightly down and toward the right edge of your lane
why: Avoid looking directly at oncoming headlights; use the right edge of your lane as a visual guide until the vehicle passes.

q: When weather makes road conditions poor, what three adjustments are recommended?
a: Reduce following distance, increase speed, and change lanes often
Allow more time, increase following distance, and reduce speed
Use cruise control, high beams, and the shoulder
Brake later, follow trucks closely, and accelerate through curves
why: Poor conditions require more time, more space and less speed.

q: Why should you increase your space cushion in bad weather?
a: To allow more time and distance to respond and stop
To prevent other vehicles from passing
why: Reduced traction and visibility increase the time and distance needed to respond safely.

q: Heavy rain sharply reduces visibility. What is the best immediate adjustment?
a: Increase speed to leave the storm sooner
Reduce speed and increase following distance
Use cruise control to hold a constant speed
Follow the vehicle ahead more closely
why: Reduced visibility and traction require less speed and more space to respond safely.

q: How far ahead should you generally scan when driving in an urban area?
why: In an urban area, look about 12 to 15 seconds ahead, roughly one to one-and-a-half blocks.

q: How far ahead should you generally scan when driving in a rural area?
why: In rural areas, look at least 20 to 25 seconds ahead to give yourself time to respond.

q: About how often should you glance in your rear-view mirrors during normal driving?
why: The guide recommends checking behind by glancing in the mirrors every 8 to 12 seconds.

q: You expect to slow for traffic ahead. What extra check should you make before braking?
why: Glancing behind before slowing helps you understand what following traffic is doing.

q: Which is an example of a fixed hazard?
a: A child running toward the road
An icy patch that forms overnight
why: A hidden driveway is a permanent roadway condition and therefore a fixed hazard.

q: Which is an example of a variable hazard?
a: A hill that blocks your view
why: School children are a variable hazard because their presence and movement change.

q: A driver is following you too closely. If it is safe, what should you do?
a: Reduce speed slightly to encourage them to pass
Move closer to the vehicle ahead
why: A slight speed reduction may encourage the tailgater to pass. If they do not, increase the space ahead of you.

q: Why should you leave extra space when stopped behind another vehicle?
a: So you can move into another lane without reversing if needed
So pedestrians can walk between the vehicles
To make the traffic light change faster
To prevent the vehicle ahead from rolling back
why: Extra space gives you an escape route and lowers the chance of being pushed into the vehicle ahead if struck from behind.

q: Under normal road and weather conditions, what minimum following time does the guide recommend for most vehicles?
why: Most drivers should remain at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead in normal conditions.

q: What minimum following time is recommended when driving a large vehicle such as a motorhome?
why: The guide recommends a minimum four-second following distance for large vehicles such as motorhomes.

q: The vehicle ahead passes a road marking. You reach it before finishing 'one-thousand-and-two.' What does this mean?
a: The vehicle ahead is driving too slowly
why: Reaching the marker before completing the two-second count means the gap is too small.

q: You miss your highway exit. What should you do?
a: Stop in your lane and wait
Make a U-turn through the median
why: Continue to the next exit. Never reverse on the roadway to return to a missed exit or turn.

q: Does using a hands-free phone eliminate the driving distraction described in the guide?
a: Only if the call is under one minute
why: The guide states that hands-free phone use can still take attention away from driving.

q: You need to send a text while driving. What is the proper action?
a: Send it at a red light
Ask traffic to wait while you type
Stop in a safe and legal place before using the phone
Hold the phone below the window line
why: Stop in a safe and legal place before making calls or sending messages.

q: According to the guide, specified distracted-driving offences include a fine and how many demerit points?
why: The listed distracted-driving offences carry three demerit points in addition to fines.

q: Which activity is listed as distracted driving?
a: Entering information into a GPS while driving
why: Entering information into a GPS while driving is one of the listed distractions.

q: Who is responsible for ensuring passengers under 16 are properly secured?
why: The driver is responsible for passengers under 16 being properly secured.

q: A child must be in a child safety seat when the child is under six years old and weighs no more than:
why: A child under six who weighs 18 kilograms (40 pounds) or less must be properly secured in a child safety seat.

q: Children who weigh more than 18 kg (40 lb) should generally use what before moving to the vehicle seat belt alone?
a: A lap belt behind the back
why: The guide recommends an approved booster seat before using the vehicle belt alone.

q: May a person ride inside a trailer while it is being towed?
why: It is against the law to let a person ride in a trailer while it is being towed.

q: May a passenger ride in the open box of a pickup truck on a roadway?
why: Drivers must not allow anyone to ride on the outside of a vehicle, including an open pickup box.

q: A load extends 1.5 metres or more beyond the rear of a vehicle during daylight. What must mark the end?
a: A red flag at least 30 cm on each side
why: During daylight, a square red flag at least 30 centimetres on each side must mark the projecting load.

q: A load extends 1.5 metres or more beyond the rear of a vehicle at night. What is required at its end?
why: At night, a red light must be attached to the end of the extension or load.

q: At a pedestrian-activated crossing with flashing yellow lights, what maximum speed applies?
why: Slow to a maximum of 30 km/h and yield to pedestrians wanting to cross.

q: A pedestrian enters an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection. What must you do?
a: Continue because there are no painted lines
Pass behind the pedestrian without slowing
why: Drivers must yield to pedestrians in both marked and unmarked crosswalks.

q: When stopping for a pedestrian at a crosswalk, about how far back should you stop so other drivers can see the pedestrian?
a: At the edge of the crosswalk
why: Stopping two to three car lengths back improves visibility for traffic in other lanes.

q: A vehicle ahead slows near a crosswalk. Should you pass it?
a: Yes, if the other lane looks clear
Only if you sound the horn
Only if the crosswalk is unmarked
why: Never pass a vehicle approaching a crosswalk; it may be stopping for a pedestrian.

q: In a residential area, why should you glance beneath parked vehicles ahead?
a: To look for children's feet, toys, or bicycle wheels
To see whether engines are running
why: Feet, toys, or bicycle wheels can warn that a child may emerge into the roadway.

q: A person walking beside and pushing a bicycle is considered:
why: A cyclist who dismounts and pushes the bicycle is treated as a pedestrian.

q: You are parked at the curb and want to open your door. What must you do first?
a: Check for cyclists and wait until it is safe
Open it quickly before a cyclist arrives
why: It is the driver's responsibility to check for cyclists before opening the door.

q: Why should you avoid following a cyclist closely?
a: Bicycles always exceed the speed limit
Cyclists do not have brake lights to warn you when they stop
Cyclists are required to turn left suddenly
why: Cyclists may slow or stop without brake lights, so drivers need extra space.

q: A motorcycle is travelling in the left portion of its lane. What should you assume?
a: It may be using that position for visibility; do not assume a turn
It is inviting you to share the lane
why: Motorcyclists often use the left part of the lane to be more visible; this does not necessarily signal a left turn.

q: May a car share a lane beside a motorcycle?
why: A motorcycle rider needs the entire lane to travel safely.

q: Why should you leave extra space behind a motorcycle?
a: Motorcycles always travel below the limit
why: Motorcycles can stop quickly and may also need to react suddenly to road hazards.

q: You are behind a large truck and cannot see both of its side mirrors. What does this indicate?
a: The truck driver can see you clearly
You are too close and may be in a blind spot
The truck is about to turn
You should flash your high beams
why: If you cannot see both side mirrors, you are too close for the truck driver to see you reliably.

q: A large truck ahead is turning right. Where should you avoid driving?
a: In the space between the truck and the curb
In a separate lane well back
Where the driver can see you
why: Large vehicles need extra turning room and can squeeze a vehicle caught on their right.

q: After passing a heavy commercial vehicle, why should you leave extra room before moving back in front?
a: The truck needs more distance to slow or stop
The truck is required to speed up
The truck's horn can damage hearing
why: Heavy vehicles need much more stopping distance, so cutting in closely is dangerous.

q: Why must you never pass a log-hauling truck while it is turning off the highway?
a: The truck may stop without lights
Logs can extend far behind and sweep across lanes
The driver cannot use brakes while turning
The truck always has the right-of-way
why: The rear logs may extend as much as nine metres and can block or sweep across multiple lanes during a turn.

q: On an undivided highway, a school bus ahead has alternating amber lights flashing. What should you do?
a: Stop only if children are visible
why: Amber lights warn that the bus is about to stop and activate its red lights.

q: About how far from a stopped school bus with flashing red lights should you stop?
why: Stop about 20 metres away, roughly four to five car lengths.

q: A school bus stops on a four-lane road with no median and activates its red lights. Who must stop?
a: Only vehicles in the bus's lane
why: On an undivided highway, traffic approaching from both directions must stop.

q: You approach from the opposite direction on a highway divided by a median. A school bus has flashing red lights. What should you do?
a: Proceed with caution and watch for pedestrians
why: On the opposite side of a divided highway, you may proceed cautiously while watching for pedestrians.

q: After stopping for a school bus, when may you proceed?
a: As soon as no children are visible
When the red lights are off and the stop sign is no longer extended
When the bus driver waves once
why: Remain stopped until the alternating red lights are off and the stop sign has retracted.

q: What reminder is associated with flashing amber and red lights on a maintenance vehicle?
why: The guide uses the reminder: flashing amber and red means snowplow ahead.

q: Why should you maintain the posted safe following distance behind a snowplow?
a: To avoid rock damage and gain reaction time
To keep the snowplow from slowing down
To prevent your engine from freezing
why: More distance gives you reaction time and protects the vehicle from rocks or sand thrown by the plow.

q: When is passing a snowplow prohibited?
a: Whenever the plow is moving below the limit
When the view beside it is obstructed or passing cannot be done safely
why: Do not pass when visibility is obstructed, the pass would impede the plow, or it cannot be completed safely.

q: At a railway crossing sign, when must you stop for an approaching train?
a: Only when the gate is down
When the train is visible or sounding a signal and is within 500 metres
When the train is within 50 metres
why: Stop when a train is visible or sounding a signal and approaching within 500 metres.

q: At a railway crossing controlled by a stop sign, where must you stop?
a: Between 1 and 3 metres from the nearest rail
Between 5 and 15 metres from the nearest rail
why: A stop sign at a railway crossing requires a full stop between five and 15 metres from the nearest rail.

q: A train has passed, but the crossing gate is still down and the red lights are flashing. What should you do?
a: Proceed if you cannot see another train
why: Stay stopped until the gate is raised, the lights stop flashing and the bells stop ringing.

q: After the last car of a train passes at a multiple-track crossing, what should you check before crossing?
a: Whether another train is approaching on another track
Whether the vehicle behind is signalling
Whether the train was carrying passengers
why: A second train may be approaching on another track, so make sure all tracks are clear.

q: After a long day, you begin drifting toward the edge of your lane. What is the safest response?
why: Lane drifting is a warning sign of fatigue. Stop safely and rest.

q: Which condition can make driver fatigue worse?
why: A warm, comfortable vehicle can intensify fatigue.

q: Which plan best reduces fatigue before a long trip?
a: Sleep well and plan rest stops
Skip meals and drive straight through
Rely on caffeine instead of sleep
Start after a full day of physical work
why: Being rested before leaving and taking breaks reduce fatigue risk.

q: A pharmacist warns that your medication may cause dizziness. What should you do before driving?
a: Wait until you know it is safe and follow medical advice
Take a smaller dose without asking
why: Know the medication's effects and follow advice from a doctor or pharmacist before driving.

q: Why is mixing alcohol with medication especially dangerous before driving?
a: It always stops the medicine working
The combined effects may increase impairment
why: Alcohol or drugs can interact with medication and increase impairment.

q: According to the guide, when can impairment begin?
a: With the first drink or drug use
Only when a driver feels impaired
why: Impairment begins with the first drink or drug use.

q: A driver says one drink cannot affect driving because they still feel normal. What is the best response?
a: Feeling normal proves driving is safe
Impairment can begin before the driver notices it
One drink matters only at night
why: Alcohol can impair judgement and reaction before the driver notices obvious effects.

q: When are demerit points recorded against a driving record?
a: When the driver is convicted of an offence
why: Demerit points are recorded when a driver is convicted of an offence.

q: A driver voluntarily pays the fine on a ticket. For demerit purposes, what does that mean?
a: The points are delayed for a year
why: Voluntarily paying the assessed fine counts as a conviction.

q: When does a fully licensed driver receive a demerit-point warning letter?
why: A fully licensed driver receives a warning at 8 to 14 points within two years.

q: How many demerit points within two years automatically suspend a fully licensed driver's privileges?
why: A fully licensed driver is automatically suspended at 15 or more points.

q: When does a GDL driver receive a demerit-point warning letter?
why: A GDL driver receives a warning at 4 to 7 points within two years.

q: After serving a GDL demerit suspension, how many points remain on the reinstated record?
why: A GDL licence is reinstated with three points remaining.

q: After serving a fully licensed driver's demerit suspension, how many points remain?
why: The licence is reinstated with seven points remaining.

q: How many demerit points apply for failing to remain at a collision scene?
why: Failing to remain at a collision scene carries seven points.

q: How many demerit points apply for failing to stop for a school bus?
