why: Failing to stop for a school bus carries six points.

q: A driver fails to yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk. How many demerit points apply?
why: This offence carries four demerit points.

q: A driver exceeds the speed limit by 20 km/h. How many demerit points apply?
why: Speeding by 16 to 30 km/h carries three points.

q: A driver exceeds the speed limit by 40 km/h. How many demerit points apply?
why: Speeding by 31 to 50 km/h carries four points.

q: A driver exceeds the speed limit by 55 km/h. How many demerit points apply?
why: Speeding by at least 51 km/h carries six points.

q: How many demerit points apply when a Class 7 learner violates the midnight-to-5-a.m. curfew?
why: The Class 7 curfew violation carries two points.

q: What is the automatic suspension length for a first demerit-point suspension?
why: The first demerit suspension is one month.

q: A driver receives a second demerit suspension within one year. How long is it?
why: A second suspension within one year is three months.

q: A driver receives a third demerit suspension within two years. How long is it?
why: A third suspension within two years is six months.

q: When are demerit points for a conviction normally removed?
a: Two years after the conviction date
why: Points are removed two years after the conviction date.

q: What credit may an approved defensive driving course provide to an eligible driver?
why: An approved course may provide a three-point credit for two years.

q: Under federal impaired-driving law, refusing a required breath or blood sample is:
why: Refusing a required breath or blood sample is an offence.

q: An officer believes a driver's ability is impaired by a medical condition. Which sanction may apply?
why: IRS: 24-hour can apply when a medical condition, alcohol, or drugs impair driving ability.

q: Someone drives while suspended. What can happen to the vehicle, even if someone else owns it?
a: It can be seized for 30 days
why: The vehicle can be seized and impounded for 30 days regardless of ownership.

q: Why must a driver keep the address on their licence current?
a: Suspension notices go to the last recorded address
why: Suspension notices are mailed to the last recorded licence address.

q: A suspension period ends, but its conditions are incomplete. May the driver resume driving?
a: No, all conditions must first be met
why: A suspension remains until every reinstatement condition is met.

q: After completing suspension requirements, where does a driver seek licence reinstatement?
why: Take proof of completed requirements to an Alberta registry agent.

q: What does an ignition interlock measure before allowing a vehicle to start?
why: The device measures alcohol concentration in the driver's breath.

q: Before towing on an Alberta road, what trailer document must the driver carry?
why: Valid trailer registration must be with the driver while towing.

q: Which trailer lights must be activated from the towing vehicle?
a: Tail-lights, brake lights, and turn signals
why: The trailer needs working tail-lights, brake lights, and turn signals.

q: Which trailers are excepted from the guide's crossed safety-chain requirement?
why: The requirement applies to all trailers except fifth-wheel trailers.

q: A trailer has an emergency breakaway system. What should be checked before departure?
a: That it is connected as the manufacturer directs
That it is tied with rope
why: Connect the breakaway system according to the manufacturer's instructions.

q: The trailer is wider than the towing vehicle. What mirror equipment is required?
why: Extension mirrors are required when the trailer is wider than the towing vehicle.

q: Which trailer is listed as not requiring brakes under the 910-kilogram rule?
why: A trailer with a gross weight of 910 kg or less is listed as not requiring brakes.

q: A trailer weighs less than half the unloaded weight of the towing vehicle. What does the guide say?
a: It is listed as not requiring brakes
Brakes are needed only in cities
why: This is one of the trailer categories listed as not requiring brakes.

q: Why should a towing driver wait for a larger gap before entering traffic?
a: Added weight and length require more time and distance
why: A towing combination is longer and accelerates more slowly.

q: How should acceleration, braking, and lane changes change while towing?
a: Accelerate and brake more slowly and allow more time
why: Added weight and length require smoother actions and additional time.

q: On a multi-lane highway, where should a slower towing vehicle normally travel?
why: Slower-moving vehicles should travel in the right lane.

q: Traffic builds behind a slow vehicle towing a trailer. What should its driver do?
a: Find a safe place off-road and allow passing
Move onto the shoulder without slowing
why: Find a safe place off the road so other traffic can pass.

q: When preparing a left turn with a trailer, where should the vehicle travel within its lane?
a: Near the right edge without entering another lane
why: Approaching near the right edge creates room for trailer off-tracking.

q: During a turn, where do trailer wheels travel compared with the towing vehicle's wheels?
why: Trailer wheels track inside the towing vehicle's wheel path.

q: What can happen if a driver fails to allow for off-tracking on a right turn?
a: The trailer may strike a curb, parked vehicle, or pedestrian
why: A trailer cuts inside the towing vehicle's path and can strike nearby hazards.

q: No guide is available before backing a trailer. What should the driver do first?
a: Walk behind the trailer and check the path
why: Walk behind the trailer and make sure the path is clear.

q: How fast should a driver reverse while backing a trailer?
why: Always reverse no faster than a walking pace.

q: While backing, you want the trailer to begin moving left. Which way should you initially steer?
why: Begin by steering opposite the desired trailer direction: right to move the trailer left.

q: Under the provincial default, when is a school zone in effect on a school day?
why: Unless different municipal times are posted, Alberta school-zone periods are 8:00-9:30 a.m., 11:30 a.m.-1:30 p.m., and 3:00-4:30 p.m. on school days.

q: A school-zone sign displays times that differ from the provincial defaults. Which times apply?
a: The times posted on the sign
why: Municipalities may set different school-zone hours; posted times govern.

q: What is the school-zone speed limit in urban and rural Alberta unless otherwise posted?
why: The default school-zone maximum is 30 km/h when the zone is in effect.

q: You are behind a vehicle travelling 25 km/h in an active school zone. May you pass it?
a: Yes, if no children are present
No, passing in the same direction is prohibited while the zone is active
Only if the road has two lanes
why: Do not pass or attempt to pass another vehicle travelling in the same direction in an active school zone.

q: You see a school sign without an attached speed sign. What have you entered?
why: A school sign without a speed sign identifies a school area; use caution because children may be nearby.

q: Under the provincial default, when are playground-zone restrictions in effect?
a: Every day from 8:30 a.m. until one hour after sunset
why: Unless different times are posted, playground-zone restrictions apply every day from 8:30 a.m. until one hour after sunset.

q: At noon on a Sunday, you enter a playground zone with no special times posted. What maximum speed applies?
why: Playground zones apply every day during their effective hours, including Sundays, and are 30 km/h unless otherwise posted.

q: A playground sign has no speed-limit sign attached. What should you do?
a: Use caution because children may be nearby
Treat it as a school zone
why: The sign marks a playground area, not a speed zone, and warns drivers to use caution.

q: The pedestrian signal changes to DON'T WALK after someone has already begun crossing. What may the pedestrian do?
a: Wait for the next WALK signal in the roadway
why: A pedestrian who began crossing before DON'T WALK appeared may continue and clear the crosswalk.

q: You face a green arrow beside a red light. Which movement is allowed without stopping?
a: Only the direction shown by the arrow
No movement until all lights are green
why: A green arrow with a red light permits movement only in the arrow's direction.

q: All approaches at an intersection display flashing red lights. How should drivers treat it?
why: When every direction flashes red, the intersection operates as a four-way stop.

q: A flashing green light faces you. What should you remember even though opposing traffic faces red?
a: You must still yield to pedestrians and vehicles lawfully in the intersection
The signal is about to fail
why: A flashing green permits through or turning movements without stopping, but lawful intersection users still have priority.

q: How close must the wheels of a parallel-parked vehicle be to the curb?
why: The law requires the wheels to be no more than 50 centimetres from the curb.

q: Before beginning a parallel park, why should you brake gradually well before the space?
a: To alert following drivers with your brake lights
why: Early gradual braking slows the vehicle and warns drivers behind through the brake lights.

q: When first positioning beside the vehicle ahead of a parallel-parking space, about how much side clearance should you leave?
why: The guide recommends about one metre between the two vehicles before reversing.

q: Before pulling out from a parallel park, which blind-spot check is especially important?
a: Over the left shoulder for traffic and cyclists
Over the right shoulder for the curb
why: Check mirrors and look over the left shoulder for traffic and cyclists not visible in the mirrors.

q: Before opening the driver's door of a curbside parked vehicle, what should you check for?
a: Traffic and cyclists approaching from behind
why: Check mirrors and the left blind spot for approaching traffic or cyclists before opening the door.

q: From which direction should you approach a vehicle parked parallel to the curb before entering it?
a: From the traffic lane side only
why: Approach from the front so you can see traffic in the nearest lane before opening the door.

q: When entering a right-side angle-parking space, about how far should you travel from the parked vehicles?
why: The guide recommends staying about 1.5 metres from the rear of the parked vehicles.

q: While leaving an angle-parking stall, who has the right-of-way?
a: Traffic and pedestrians behind the parked vehicle
why: A driver backing from a parking stall must yield to traffic and pedestrians.

q: A vehicle beside you blocks your view while you reverse from an angle stall. What should you do?
a: Reverse quickly through the blind area
Move slowly, stop when needed, and check once you can see past it
Honk and assume others will stop
Turn immediately into the travel lane
why: Reverse slowly and be prepared to stop until you can see traffic and pedestrians beyond the obstructing vehicle.

q: Where may you enter a perpendicular or angle stall located to your left?
why: The guide says to enter a left-side perpendicular or angle stall only in a parking lot.

q: Why is a left-side 90-degree parking stall often easier to enter than a right-side stall?
a: It has a wider painted space
There is more room to achieve the proper turning angle
The steering wheel turns farther left
why: Approaching from the opposite side of the aisle provides more room to establish the proper angle, but oncoming traffic must be checked.

q: You technically have right-of-way, but another driver is not yielding. What should you do?
a: Do everything possible to prevent a collision
why: Right-of-way rules do not remove your responsibility to prevent a collision.

q: A peace officer directs you to stop while your traffic light is green. Which instruction controls?
why: Directions from a peace or police officer take priority over signs and signals.

q: With no stop line or marked crosswalk, how close to the intersecting roadway must you stop?
why: Stop within three metres of the intersecting roadway without interfering with pedestrians.

q: You approach a yield sign and see no traffic or pedestrians requiring you to yield. Must you stop?
a: No, you may proceed cautiously without a complete stop
Only if another vehicle is behind you
why: A yield sign requires slowing and yielding as needed, but not a stop when the way is clear.

q: At an uncontrolled T-intersection, does the vehicle travelling straight automatically have right-of-way?
a: No; the vehicle on the right has right-of-way
why: At an uncontrolled T-intersection, the normal rule still applies: yield to the vehicle on your right.

q: When leaving an alley across a sidewalk, where must you stop first?
a: Only if a pedestrian is visible
why: When exiting an alley, driveway, parking lot, or service road, stop before crossing the sidewalk and yield to pedestrians.

q: Do right-of-way rules apply at unmarked intersections in parking lots?
a: Only when a security guard is present
why: Parking lots contain uncontrolled intersections where normal right-of-way rules apply.

q: A vehicle ahead has stopped at an unmarked crosswalk for a pedestrian. May you pass it?
a: Yes, if the other lane is clear
No, do not pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian
why: Every intersection has marked or unmarked crosswalks, and you must not pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian.

q: In which direction does traffic circulate around an Alberta roundabout's centre island?
a: The direction shown by the nearest vehicle
why: Traffic circulates counterclockwise around the centre island.

q: When should you activate the right signal to take a later exit from a roundabout?
a: After passing the exit immediately before yours
why: Signal right after passing the exit before the one you intend to use.

q: You plan to take the first exit from a two-lane roundabout. Which approach lane should you use?
why: Approach in the right lane, stay right in the circle, and exit into the right lane.

q: You plan to travel past the first exit of a two-lane roundabout. Which lane should you generally use?
a: Any lane followed by a lane change inside
why: Drivers travelling past the first exit should use the left lane and remain in it through the circle.

q: While in a two-lane roundabout, you realize you cannot exit safely. What should you do?
a: Continue around in your lane and try again
why: Do not stop or cut across lanes; remain in your lane and travel around again.

q: You are exiting from the left lane of a roundabout. What must you check immediately before crossing the outside lane?
a: Traffic in the right lane continuing around
Only traffic behind the centre island
why: Check for vehicles in the right lane that may continue around before crossing that lane to exit.

q: How far in advance should you normally be established in the proper turning lane?
why: The guide recommends being in the proper turning lane at least 15 metres before the intersection.

q: Before turning right, why should you check over your right shoulder?
a: To detect cyclists and pedestrians approaching the intersection
To check the rear licence plate
To see whether the curb is painted
why: A right shoulder check helps detect cyclists and pedestrians in the curb-side blind area.

q: A parked vehicle is close to the corner in the curb lane you would normally enter. Where should you turn?
a: Behind the parked vehicle regardless of space
Into the first available lane left of the obstruction after yielding
why: When an obstruction is close to the corner, turn into the first available lane to its left and yield to traffic already using that lane.

q: You must wait in an intersection before completing a left turn. How should your front wheels be positioned?
why: Keep the wheels straight so a rear impact does not push the vehicle into oncoming traffic.

q: Before turning left from a two-lane highway, which extra check is important?
a: A left shoulder check for a vehicle passing you
A right shoulder check for parked cars
why: Check over the left shoulder to ensure another vehicle is not passing on your left.

q: Turning left from a two-way road onto a one-way road, which lane should you enter?
a: The first available lane on the left
why: Turn from the lane nearest the yellow line into the first available lane on the left side of the one-way road.

q: Turning left from a one-way road onto a two-way road, which lane should you enter?
a: The nearest lane to the right of the yellow line
why: Turn from the left lane into the nearest lane to the right of the yellow centre line.

q: When are dual-lane turns permitted?
a: Only where signs or pavement markings indicate them
why: Dual-lane turns may be made only where signs or pavement markings designate them.

q: While making a marked dual-lane turn, may you change lanes in the intersection?
a: No, stay in the corresponding lane
Only if the other vehicle slows
why: Maintain the corresponding lane throughout a dual turn; another vehicle may be turning beside you.

q: When should you enter a shared two-way left-turn lane?
a: Close to where you intend to turn
why: Enter the shared centre lane only near the point where you will turn left.

q: May you make a U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection without a sign specifically permitting it?
why: A U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection is prohibited unless a traffic-control device permits it.

q: In an urban area, may you make a U-turn at an alley intersection?
a: Only if no traffic is present
why: Urban U-turns are prohibited at alley intersections.

q: On a rural road near a hill crest, when is a U-turn prohibited?
a: When another driver within 150 metres cannot see you approaching from either direction
Only when the speed limit exceeds 80 km/h
Only when a centre line is present
why: Near a rural hill crest, a U-turn is prohibited where another approaching driver within 150 metres cannot see you.

q: What does a warning sign showing a T-shaped intersection tell you?
a: The road ends at another road ahead
why: A T-intersection warning means the road you are on ends at another roadway.

q: A yellow sign shows a side road joining from the right. What should you anticipate?
a: A hidden road and possible entering traffic
why: The sign warns that a road joins from the right and traffic may enter.

q: How does a free-flow added-lane sign differ from a merge sign?
a: The entering lane continues instead of immediately joining
It requires every vehicle to stop
why: A free-flow sign shows roadways running side-by-side without immediately merging.

q: You see a ROAD NARROWS sign. What should you do?
a: Prepare for less roadway width ahead
Increase speed before the narrow section
why: The warning indicates reduced roadway width; adjust speed and position as needed.

q: A sign warns that the right lane ends. What is the proper response?
a: Plan a safe lane change before the lane ends
Force traffic in the through lane to stop
why: Check traffic, signal, and merge safely before the lane ends.

q: What does a DIVIDED HIGHWAY ENDS sign warn you about?
a: Opposing traffic will no longer be separated by a median
why: The physical divider ends and opposing traffic will be closer.

q: A bridge-ices warning appears on a cold day. Why should you slow before the bridge?
a: Bridges may freeze before the roadway
Bridges always have lower speed limits
why: Cold air surrounds bridge decks, so they can become icy before nearby roads.

q: What do chevron signs along a road indicate?
a: A sharp bend and its direction
why: Chevrons mark a sharp change in road direction.

q: A sign says cyclists may use the full lane because it is too narrow for side-by-side travel. What should a driver do?
a: Treat the cyclist as entitled to the lane and pass only when safe
Sound the horn until the cyclist moves
Use the bicycle lane to pass
why: The lane is too narrow for safe side-by-side travel; allow the cyclist full use of it.

q: What information does a highway route marker provide?
a: The road's route number or designation
why: Route markers identify roads by number, name, or designation.

q: Which background colour commonly identifies off-road services such as fuel or accommodation?
why: Blue information signs identify services and facilities.

q: A slow-moving vehicle emblem is used on vehicles normally travelling below what speed?
why: The emblem marks vehicles that travel at less than 40 km/h.

q: A construction-zone speed limit is posted, but no workers are visible. Must you obey it?
why: Construction-zone limits apply at all times because hazards may remain when workers are absent.

q: When are fines doubled in an Alberta construction zone?
a: Only when a lane is closed
why: Fines are doubled when workers are present.

q: A flag person gives directions that differ from the normal lane markings. What should you do?
why: Obey authorized flag-person directions in construction areas.

q: What do yellow pavement lines separate?
a: Traffic moving in the same direction
why: Yellow lines separate opposing traffic and should normally be on the driver's left.

q: What do white pavement lines separate?
a: Traffic moving in the same direction
why: White lines separate lanes travelling in the same direction.

q: A broken yellow centre line is on your side. When may you pass?
a: Whenever you are below the speed limit
Only when the lane is clear and the pass can be completed safely
why: A broken yellow line permits passing only when the manoeuvre is otherwise legal and safe.

q: A solid yellow line is beside a broken yellow line. Which driver may pass?
a: Only the driver with the broken line on their side
Only the driver with the solid line
why: Passing is permitted only from the side with the broken yellow line.

q: What does a solid white lane line indicate?
a: The lane is reserved for buses
why: A solid white line means drivers should not change lanes across it.

q: What does a broken white lane line indicate?
a: Lane changing is permitted when safe
why: A broken white line permits lane changes when they can be made safely.

q: What do pavement arrows tell drivers?
a: Which movements are permitted from the lane
why: Lane arrows regulate or guide the movements allowed from that lane.

q: What does a diamond painted in a traffic lane normally indicate?
a: The lane is reserved for specified vehicles
why: Diamond markings identify reserved lanes, with signs explaining applicable vehicles or times.

q: When may a motor vehicle enter a marked bicycle lane?
a: When necessary to turn or enter or exit parking
why: Motor vehicles may enter a bicycle lane only as needed for a turn or to enter or leave parking, while yielding appropriately.

q: What do large X pavement markings on a rural highway warn about?
why: X markings on rural highways warn of an approaching railway crossing.

q: Before entering your vehicle, what should a walk-around include?
a: Checking for people, obstacles, tire problems, and fluid leaks
why: A walk-around helps find children, pedestrians, obstacles, tire issues, leaks, and other hazards.

q: How should your elbows be positioned when your hands are correctly placed on the steering wheel?
why: A comfortable position leaves the elbows slightly bent and maintains control.

q: How should the inside rear-view mirror normally be adjusted?
a: To frame as much of the rear window as possible
why: Frame the rear window to show as much of the area behind as possible.

q: Why are outside mirrors adjusted to show only a small portion of your own vehicle?
a: To reduce blind spots while keeping a reference point
To make parking lines appear wider
why: This positioning helps reduce blind areas, but shoulder checks are still required.

q: Before moving away from the right curb, what sequence is safest?
a: Signal left, check mirrors and blind spot, then move when clear
why: Check the path and mirrors, shoulder-check the blind spot, signal left, and enter traffic only when safe.

q: Which automatic-transmission position locks the transmission for parking?
why: Park locks the transmission and is used when starting the engine and leaving the vehicle parked.

q: In which automatic-transmission positions can the engine normally start?
why: The guide states the engine starts in Park or Neutral, not in driving gears.

q: Why might a driver select a lower automatic-transmission gear on a steep hill?
a: For more power at lower speed and to limit upshifting
To coast with no engine control
why: Lower gears provide more power at lower speed and can help control the vehicle on hills or loose surfaces.

q: What happens when the clutch pedal is pressed fully down?
a: Engine power is disconnected from the transmission and wheels
why: Pressing the clutch disengages the engine from the transmission so gears can be changed.

q: What is the friction point in a manual vehicle?
a: Where the clutch begins reconnecting the engine and transmission
Where the brakes begin to lock
Where the steering reaches full turn
why: The friction point is where the clutch begins transmitting engine power as the pedal is released.

q: Why should you avoid resting your foot on the clutch pedal while driving?
why: Unnecessary contact with the clutch pedal is riding the clutch and causes extra wear.

q: What steering-wheel hand position is generally recommended?
why: The recommended position is approximately 9 and 3 o'clock for control and safety.

q: As the steering wheel returns after a turn, may it slide through your hands?
a: Yes, with a loosened grip while maintaining contact
Only with one hand off the wheel
why: The wheel may slide back through a light grip, but the driver should maintain contact and control.

q: Which three common movements require a signal?
a: Leaving the curb, turning, and changing lanes
Starting the engine, stopping, and accelerating
why: Signal when moving from the curb or parking lane, turning, or changing lanes.

q: Your turn signal does not cancel after completing a turn. What should you do?
a: Leave it on until the next turn
why: Cancel a signal that does not switch off automatically so other drivers are not misled.

q: Why can driving much slower than traffic be hazardous?
a: It disrupts traffic flow and can increase collision risk
It shortens stopping distance for everyone
why: Unnecessarily slow driving disrupts traffic flow and can create conflicts.

q: What three distances make up total stopping distance?
why: Total stopping distance equals perception distance plus reaction distance plus braking distance.

q: What is perception time?
a: The time needed to recognize and understand a need to stop
The time needed to move a foot to the brake
The time the brakes take to stop the vehicle
The time needed to restart after stopping
why: Perception time is the interval needed to detect and understand a hazard.

q: What is reaction time?
a: The time needed to move from the accelerator to the brake after recognizing danger
The time brakes take to stop the wheels
The time needed to scan an intersection
The time needed to steer around a hazard
why: Reaction time begins after the hazard is understood and ends when braking action starts.

q: Which driver-controlled factor can increase stopping distance before the brakes are even applied?
a: Fatigue that slows perception and reaction
why: Fatigue reduces alertness and decision speed, increasing perception and reaction distance.

q: For a normal stop, when should you begin braking?
a: When the wheels begin to skid
why: Brake early so enough distance remains and the stop can be smooth and controlled.

q: How can you finish a normal stop smoothly?
a: Ease brake pressure slightly, then reapply just before stopping
why: Slightly releasing and then reapplying brake pressure helps prevent a jerky final stop.

q: What is threshold braking in a vehicle without ABS?
a: Maximum braking without locking the wheels
Braking only with the rear wheels
why: Threshold braking applies the greatest useful pressure while retaining steering control.

q: At what speed should ordinary reversing be done?
a: A crawl or slow walking speed
why: All reversing should be done at a crawl or slow walking speed.

q: While reversing left, where should you mainly look?
a: Over the left shoulder, with frequent glances forward
why: Look in the direction the rear is travelling and continue checking the front for clearance.

q: A driver's licence shows condition A. What must the driver use when driving?
why: Condition A means adequate lenses are required.

q: Which licence code means Special Conditions?
why: B identifies special conditions.

q: Which condition code requires periodic medical reporting?
why: C means periodic medical.

q: A licence displays condition D. What periodic report is required?
why: D means periodic vision report.

q: What does condition E require periodically?
why: E means periodic driver examination.

q: Condition F appears on a licence. What does it identify?
why: F means valid temporary licence.

q: Which condition code identifies a temporary resident?
why: G identifies temporary resident status.

q: A licence displays H. Which trip would violate that condition?
why: H restricts the driver to daylight driving.

q: A licence shows J. What vehicle equipment does the driver require?
why: J means outside mirrors are required.

q: A driver with condition K may operate which transmission type?
why: K restricts the driver to automatic transmission vehicles.

q: Which condition code means hand controls?
why: L means hand controls.

q: What does condition M indicate?
a: Under Transportation and Economic Corridors review
why: M indicates the driver is under Transportation and Economic Corridors review.

q: A licence has condition N. Which classes are excluded?
why: N excludes Class 2 and Class 4 vehicles.

q: Condition P means testing must be conducted by whom?
why: P means testing by a Provincial Examiner only.

q: Which condition code means Special Medical?
why: T means special medical.

q: A driver completes approved air-brake training. Which endorsement is added?
why: Q is the air-brake endorsement.

q: Which endorsement code identifies school-bus qualification?
why: S is the school-bus endorsement.

q: A licence displays endorsement U. What training has the driver completed?
why: U records completion of an approved driver education course.

q: What does endorsement V permit?
why: V is the endorsement for extended-length vehicle combinations.

q: What is the clearest difference between a condition code and an endorsement code?
a: A condition limits or requires something; an endorsement records added training or permission
A condition is optional; an endorsement is always a penalty
Endorsements apply only to medical requirements
why: Conditions identify restrictions or requirements, while endorsements identify added qualifications, training, or permissions.
